scenes.narration: This slide puts two target-selection patterns side by side. On the left, cross-zone load balancing allows a load balancer node to forward to eligible healthy targets across enabled Availability Zones. Follow the multicolored arrows from the node to targets in three zones. That can share uneven target capacity more effectively. On the right, cross-zone forwarding is disabled, so each node directs traffic toward eligible targets in its own zone. Each participating zone therefore needs enough healthy capacity for the traffic it receives. The lower-left controls panel highlights that defaults vary by load balancer type and configuration: ALB generally enables cross-zone routing, with supported target-group options; NLB and GWLB have different defaults. Always inspect the actual effective setting. In the lower-right panel, the traffic globe and coins remind us that cross-zone target distribution is separate from where DNS sends clients, and applicable inter-zone transfer pricing and capacity tradeoffs must be checked. Cross-zone routing does not make a multi-AZ application magically resilient. Surviving targets and dependencies still need enough healthy capacity after a zone fails.

scenes.narration: The slide asks whether a load balancer health check tells the truth about the application. Start in the upper-left probe panel. A target group can test a configured protocol, port and HTTP path, with success codes, intervals and thresholds. A socket that accepts connections does not necessarily mean the application is ready. Now look at the upper-right panel showing different health states. A timeout, a response-code mismatch, an unhealthy target and an unused target each point to different troubleshooting questions. Read the actual reason code before changing routes or security groups. In the lower-left diagram, every target depends on one shared database. If a readiness probe fails whenever that shared dependency fails, the entire target group can become unhealthy at once, potentially creating a cascading outage. The lower-right warning explains ALB fail-open behavior: when all registered targets are unhealthy across enabled zones, ALB can still send requests to them. Unhealthy is not a guaranteed traffic block. Design readiness checks to express useful application service, while preserving defense-in-depth security and resilience for shared dependencies.

scenes.narration: This diagram shows why an Application Load Balancer works at the application layer. Start on the left with the incoming HTTP request. Listener rules may inspect the host name, URL path, selected headers, method, query string and source IP. Specific rules should be ordered thoughtfully before broader matches, because priority controls which matching rule wins. Follow the arrows across to the action panel. A request can be forwarded to one or more supported target groups, redirected, such as from HTTP to HTTPS, or answered with a fixed response. The default rule catches traffic that matches none of the specific conditions. In the lower-left, HTTP Two and WebSocket upgrade support illustrate that this is more than a basic TCP port switch. Once a WebSocket connection is established, messages use the selected connection and target. Finally inspect the example on the lower right: requests for shop dot example dot com slash checkout can reach checkout servers, while slash catalog reaches a separate group, without adding another public ALB. Routing selects a destination; it is not itself application authorization.
